name: Newcomb's Paradox
statement: Two rules of rational choice, dominance and expected value, give opposite answers to the same decision.
meaning: Newcomb's paradox is a decision puzzle in which two standard principles of rational choice conflict. A reliable predictor has already put money in two boxes: a transparent box holds a small sure sum, and an opaque box holds a large sum, but only if the predictor foresaw that you would take the opaque box alone. You choose between taking both boxes or only the opaque one. One line of reasoning says take both; another says take only one; and each seems compellingly rational, so the paradox is that rationality appears to speak with two voices.
mechanism: The setup pits two principles against each other. The dominance principle notes that the predictor has already acted and the boxes' contents are fixed: whatever is in the opaque box, taking both boxes yields the extra sure sum, so two-boxing dominates. The expected-value principle notes that the predictor is reliable, so one-boxers almost always find the large sum and two-boxers almost always find only the small one; conditional on your choice, one-boxing has the higher expected payoff. Because your decision is correlated with a prediction already made, the two principles come apart, and which one governs turns on how causation and evidence bear on rational choice.

examples.text: A transparent box holds a thousand dollars; an opaque box holds a million if the predictor expected you to take it alone, and nothing otherwise. You may take both boxes or only the opaque one.
Since the predictor is almost always right, those who take only the opaque box nearly always walk away with a million, so one-boxing has the far higher expected return.
The money is already in or out of the opaque box and cannot change now, so taking both boxes gets you whatever it holds plus the sure thousand: a dominating strategy.

variants.name: Causal decision theory
variants.text: The framework that sides with the two-boxer: rational choice should track the causal consequences of your act, and since your choice cannot affect the already-fixed contents, you should take both boxes.

variants.name: Evidential decision theory
variants.text: The framework that sides with the one-boxer: rational choice should maximise expected value conditional on your act as evidence, and choosing one box is strong evidence the million is there.

whyItMatters: It is a central test case in decision theory, dividing the field into causal and evidential camps and forcing precision about how prediction, correlation, and causation bear on rational choice. Its structure recurs in real problems of cooperation, commitment, and prediction, and it remains a benchmark against which theories of rationality are measured, including in recent work on decision-making by predictable agents.

working.text: recognise that dominance and expected-value reasoning genuinely diverge here, which is the source of the puzzle rather than a mistake in either.

working.lead: Ask what the choice can affect
working.text: notice that your decision cannot causally change the already-fixed contents, yet is strongly correlated with them: the crux dividing causal and evidential theorists.
commit to whether rationality tracks causal consequences or evidential expectations, since Newcomb's problem forces the choice and neither answer is uncontested.

limits: It is an unresolved problem with no consensus: able philosophers defend one-boxing and two-boxing, and the split between causal and evidential decision theory persists. Some argue the scenario is underspecified or even incoherent (that a truly infallible predictor and genuine free choice sit uneasily together), so part of the dispute concerns whether the problem is well posed. The verdict one reaches depends on prior commitments about causation and rationality that the problem itself does not settle, which is why it functions as a probe rather than a solvable exercise.
misreadings: It is not a simple maths error with an obvious right answer: sophisticated theorists land on opposite sides, and the disagreement is principled. It does not require backward causation: the predictor's accuracy can rest on ordinary prediction, not on your choice reaching back in time. And it is not merely academic; its logic underlies real dilemmas of prediction and commitment where a rational agent's choice is correlated with what others have already anticipated.
origin: Devised by the physicist William Newcomb around 1960 and brought to philosophical attention by Robert Nozick in 'Newcomb's Problem and Two Principles of Choice' (1969); it became the founding puzzle of the debate between causal and evidential decision theory.
